channel.title: Said & Checked: Wyoming — AskAmerica
channel.description: What officeholders said each day from or about Wyoming, and which statements government data supports, contradicts or rules out.

item.title: Said & Checked, Wyoming, 2026-11-20: none false or contradicted, 6 unsettled (Chuck Grassley, John Barrasso)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsettled

  • Chuck Grassley, U.S. Senator: “there is a road in Colorado that took 13 years to build due to Federal permitting delays; another project in Wyoming, a wind project, that waited 12 years for Federal approval; and a mine in Minnesota that took 12 years…” Unsettled. A Colorado Politics op-ed says Interstate 70's expansion took 13 years of environmental review before work began, and the Permitting Council's page for the Chokecherry and Sierra Madre wind project in Wyoming shows it proposed in 2008 with a federal decision in 2012 and later phase approvals; neither project was confirmed as the one meant, and the 12-year wait is not established.
  • John Barrasso, U.S. Senator: “This is the largest investment in the Nation's history in rural healthcare.” Unsettled. KFF Health News quotes experts saying the $50 billion fund appears unrivaled among limited rural programs, but Medicare and Medicaid spending in rural areas far exceeds it, and the postwar Hill-Burton hospital program has been estimated at $47 billion to $109 billion in today's dollars, so the ranking depends on what is counted.
  • John Barrasso, U.S. Senator: “Just last month, I joined our Governor Mark Gordon to announce how Wyoming is using its $205 million coming from this fund.” Unsettled. CMS's first-year award to Wyoming was $205.0 million, and a CMS release on Wyoming's plans quotes both Gov. Gordon and Sen. Barrasso, but no source read confirms that they announced it together or when.

item.title: Said & Checked, Wyoming, 2026-11-18: none false or contradicted, 1 unsupported, 2 unsettled (John Barrasso)
item.description:
No statement was found false or contradicted.

Unsupported and Unsettled

  • John Barrasso, U.S. Senator from Wyoming: “For the first 227 years under our Constitution--1789 to 2016--this Senate confirmed 94 percent of judicial nominees by unanimous consent.” Unsupported. No published count of judicial nominees confirmed by unanimous consent from 1789 to 2016 was found. Searched: AskAmerica's judge and nomination tables (no vote-method data before 2017; nominations cover recent Congresses only) and one web search, which returned Supreme Court figures only. Senate historical records and academic studies were not searched further.
  • John Barrasso, U.S. Senator from Wyoming: “This Republican Senate has already confirmed judges at the fastest pace in decades.” Unsettled. AskAmerica's nominations data count 58 circuit, district and trade-court confirmations through Nov. 17, 2026, against 82 at the same point of Trump's first term (Nov. 18, 2018) and 83 of Biden's (Nov. 18, 2022). The rows behind these counts could not be read directly, and 'pace' could also mean speed per nomination, so the claim is not settled here.
  • John Barrasso, U.S. Senator from Wyoming: “Today, more judges who are serving in the Federal courts were nominated by President Trump compared to any other recent President.” Unsettled. In AskAmerica's Federal Judicial Center data, Trump appointees outnumber every other recent president's among active judges (279 against Obama's 211). Counting judges on senior status as serving, Obama leads 291 to 280. The statement does not say which reading it means.
